question: What actually decides a person's blood group?
explanation: Think of antigens as tiny ID tags on the surface of your red blood cells. These tags are what determine your specific blood group! [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h1)

question: Why does the body's immune system sometimes react strongly against a foreign blood type?

options.A: It digests the extra plasma proteins
options.B: It tries to produce more platelets
options.C: It recognizes foreign antigens as invaders
options.D: It lacks enough red blood cells

explanation: Your immune system is like a security guard. If it sees unfamiliar ID tags (antigens) on red blood cells, it treats them like intruders and sounds the alarm. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h1)

question: If a patient has blood group O, which antibodies are floating in their plasma?
explanation: Group O red cells don't have A or B tags. Because of this, the body naturally builds up antibodies against both A and B just in case! [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h2)

question: A patient with blood group AB has which antigens sitting on their red blood cells?
explanation: The name says it all! Blood group AB means the red cells proudly wear both A and B ID tags on their surface. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h2)

question: What makes a person's blood type Rh-positive?

options.D: Absence of all red cell proteins

explanation: The plus sign (+) in a blood type comes from the RhD antigen. If it's present on the red cells, the blood is Rh-positive! [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h3)

question: When does an Rh-negative person typically develop anti-Rh antibodies?

options.A: Whenever they catch a viral infection
options.B: Automatically at six months of age

explanation: Rh antibodies aren't there from birth. They only show up if an Rh-negative person gets exposed to Rh-positive blood, like during a transfusion or pregnancy. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h3)

question: What is the main goal of doing a crossmatch test before a blood transfusion?

options.A: To determine the patient's baseline hemoglobin level
options.B: To measure the exact volume of blood needed
options.C: To sterilize the blood product before transfusion
options.D: To check for compatibility between donor and recipient

explanation: A crossmatch is like a safety rehearsal in the lab. We mix a little of the donor's and recipient's blood to make sure they get along before giving it to the patient. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h4)

question: In forward blood typing, what are we trying to identify on the patient's red blood cells?
explanation: Forward typing uses known lab solutions to hunt for the specific antigen tags sitting right on the patient's red blood cells. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h4)

question: Why is O negative blood often called the universal red cell donor?

options.A: It contains high levels of clotting factors
options.B: It lacks major red cell antigens
options.C: It can be stored longer than other types
options.D: It has the highest concentration of platelets

explanation: O negative red cells are like chameleons—they don't carry A, B, or Rh tags, so almost any patient's immune system will accept them without attacking! [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h5)

question: Which blood type is known as the universal red cell recipient?
explanation: AB positive folks already have A, B, and Rh antigens, so their plasma doesn't make antibodies against those tags. They can safely receive red cells from any ABO group! [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h5)

question: What actually happens inside the body during a hemolytic transfusion reaction?

options.A: Platelets multiply rapidly in the veins
options.B: White blood cells consume all plasma proteins
options.C: Donor red blood cells are destroyed
options.D: Hemoglobin levels rise above normal limits

explanation: If a mismatch happens, the recipient's antibodies attack the donor red cells, causing them to break apart (hemolyze) in the bloodstream. That's why crossmatching is so crucial! [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h6)

question: Which condition can happen when an Rh-negative mother carries an Rh-positive baby?
explanation: If the baby's Rh-positive cells sneak into an Rh-negative mother's circulation, her antibodies can form and attack a future baby's red blood cells. Fortunately, we can prevent this easily with routine care! [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h6)
